fact_sheet.business_description: Delphi Corporation is an automotive components and systems supplier currently operating in Chapter 11 bankruptcy [D01]. The company maintains a manufacturing footprint and engineering relationships that may hold going-concern value, though its legacy capital structure is impaired [D01].
segments_and_separable_assets: Not in pack; consolidated reporting provided without specific segment EBITDA or asset valuation evidence [D01].
economics_vs_peers: Operating margin was -21.1% in Q1 2009 compared to -5.1% in Q1 2008 [D03]. Revenue declined 51.9% in Q1 2009 vs Q1 2008 [D03]. The comparison set is reorganizing auto suppliers, not debt-free manufacturers [D06].
capital_structure: DIP financing as of May 29: ~$230m (Tranche A), ~$311m (Tranche B), and $2.75bn (Tranche C) [D04]. Proposed incremental $250m GM-supported subordinated DIP [D04]. $13,435m in compromised liabilities as of March 31 [D04].

shareholder_base_and_liquidity: 564,637,307 old common shares outstanding as of March 31, 2009, which are not representative of prospective reorganized equity [D01].

gate2.variant_view: The market views Delphi's reliance on GM for financing and production as a terminal risk amidst severe cash burn and bankruptcy uncertainty [D03, D05]. The June 16 financing hearing will serve as the catalyst to clarify recovery and eliminate the current discount driven by liquidation fears [D03, D07].

The proposed $250m GM-supported DIP financing provides necessary bridge liquidity, signaling alignment between the key customer and the restructuring process [D04, D07].
The court-supervised Chapter 11 process mitigates reliance on legacy management and provides a structured environment for realizing recovery value [D07].

final.memo:
Delphi Corporation is an automotive components supplier trapped in a Chapter 11 bankruptcy process that the market currently discounts due to extreme liquidation fears [D01, D03]. The mispricing is driven by a focus on the company's $13,435m in compromised liabilities and a Q1 2009 operating margin of -21.1%, leading investors to ignore the underlying value of the firm's engineering relationships and manufacturing footprint [D03, D04].

While the company faces severe headwinds, including a 51.9% revenue decline in Q1 2009, the GM-supported restructuring path provides a clear framework for value creation [D03]. We benchmark this against other reorganizing auto suppliers, betting that the post-event earnings power will be significantly higher than the current distressed valuation suggests [D06].

The market’s pessimism is fueled by the firm’s dependence on General Motors and a perceived lack of liquidity, but this ignores the active, court-supervised restructuring process currently underway [D05, D07]. We expect the situation to change rapidly as the court evaluates the proposed $250m incremental DIP financing [D07].

Our plan is to capitalize on the June 16, 2009 financing hearing, which serves as the primary catalyst [D07]. We are monitoring the bankruptcy court’s progress and the alignment between Delphi, GM, and the lenders [D07]. Our role is that of a distressed creditor, positioning for the recovery value inherent in the firm's going-concern footprint [D01].

Risks are concentrated in the auto sector and the binary nature of the financing hearing [D05, D06]. Our downside is protected by the court-supervised process, though a failure to secure the $250m DIP at the hearing would represent a material break in our thesis [D07]. We would exit immediately if support from GM is withdrawn or if the court-sanctioned path fails [D03, D07].

We are initiating a position in Delphi bonds at 3% of NAV, reflecting our high conviction in the court-led restructuring outcome. We will hedge our auto-industry beta using GM CDS and index puts to isolate our exposure to the idiosyncratic recovery of the company [D05].
